units.title: On-policy generation and the sequence policy gradient
outcomes: Derive the sequence policy gradient from the autoregressive factorization with a fixed prompt distribution.
Identify the distribution that actually generated a completion and the log probabilities its update requires.
units.why: The sequence objective is familiar REINFORCE, but generation now owns the sampling distribution. A correct loss on text drawn from a different decoding policy is not an on-policy estimator.

next.note: Turn the sequence derivative into a masked token loss.

study.title: RLHF Book: sequence policy gradient
study.locator: Chapter 6, The Role of Reinforcement Learning in RLHF and Deriving the Policy Gradient, equations 9 to 18 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 3: RL Motivation and Math
study.locator: Slides 20 to 28: differentiating the expectation, trajectory factorization and the token-log-probability sum
study.depth: Build on the earlier likelihood-ratio identity and Decoding policies: from greedy to nucleus sampling. Skip the classical RL review before slide 20.

focus: For a fixed prompt distribution and parameter-independent reward, \(\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}[R(x,y)\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})]\). Include the sampled stopping action when EOS ends the response.
The prompt distribution and deterministic append transition have zero parameter derivative. The completion distribution does not.
Temperature and truncation change the policy, not just its presentation. Start with untruncated categorical sampling at temperature 1; otherwise define and score the transformed policy explicitly.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, enumerate a two-token binary policy with independent tokens, each with probability \(p\) of 1, and reward 1 only for two ones. Derive \(J(p)=p^2\) and recover \(dJ/dp=2p\) from the expected score-function estimator. At \(p=1/2\), both give 1. This oracle needs only CPU arithmetic.
traps: Backpropagating the mean of frozen verifier scores. It has no path to policy parameters; the score-function loss supplies that path.
Calling a completion on-policy because its model weights match. Top-p filtering, temperature, dropout and numerical backend differences can still change its distribution.

selfTest.q: Why is there no explicit trajectory probability multiplying each sampled gradient?
selfTest.a: Sampling already weights trajectories by their probability. Multiplying by that probability again estimates a different expectation.

selfTest.q: Does the sequence gradient require gradients through sampled token IDs?
selfTest.a: No. Hold the sampled IDs fixed and differentiate their log probabilities under the policy.

selfTest.q: Can raw model log probabilities describe nucleus sampling exactly?
selfTest.a: No. The sampler removes tokens and renormalizes the retained probabilities. Raw log probabilities omit that transformation and its support restriction.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the sequence-gradient oracle and the generation-policy contract in policylab's rollout collector.
units.stopWhen: Your enumeration matches the analytic derivative for several probabilities, and you can name the sampler and scoring distribution for every rollout.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 3 supply the derivation; the mini-project supplies an exact finite-policy oracle and sampling-contract practice.

units.title: Terminal rewards, per-token loss assignment and token-space REINFORCE
outcomes: Derive why an undiscounted terminal reward weights every generated token in REINFORCE.
Implement a completion-summed loss with detached rewards and test its token gradients.
units.why: A terminal score must reach the whole completion, not just its last token. The loss reduction decides whether you optimize expected sequence reward or a length-reweighted surrogate.

next.note: Replace the broadcast return with prefix-dependent advantages.

study.title: RLHF Book: REINFORCE in token space
study.locator: Chapter 6, REINFORCE, then Implementation: Policy-Gradient Basics and Related: MDP vs. Bandit Framing (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 4: summed token log probabilities
study.locator: Slides 8 to 12: log-probability shift, gather, completion sum and REINFORCE loss
study.depth: Use a fixed or previously fitted baseline first. Slide 12's current-batch mean includes each sample's own reward; it is not an action-independent baseline. The RLOO unit checks that distinction.

focus: With terminal reward only and \(\gamma=1\), every completion token has return \(R\). Broadcasting this return is not a claim that each token independently caused the outcome.
Use \(L=-B^{-1}\sum_i A_i\sum_t m_{i,t}\log\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x_i,y_{i,<t})\). A variable per-response token mean changes the weighting.
Build on Masks, sequence log probabilities and Log-probability oracles and prompt separation. Rewards, baselines and sampled IDs are fixed; selected current log probabilities carry gradients.
units.reproduce: On CPU, use `torch.float64` selected log probabilities `[[-1., -2., -9.], [-3., -8., -7.]]`, completion masks `[[1., 1., 0.], [1., 0., 0.]]` and detached advantages `[2., -1.]`. Sum tokens, average the two sequence losses and obtain loss 1.5. Gradients with respect to selected log probabilities are `[[-1., -1., 0.], [0.5, 0., 0.]]` within floating-point tolerance.
traps: Putting the loss only on EOS because the reward arrived there. Reward placement and gradient assignment are different operations.
Replacing the token sum with a token mean without naming the changed objective. Variable response lengths make this more than a fixed learning-rate rescaling.
Reading a lower frozen-rollout loss as better generation. Only fresh, independently scored outputs establish behavior change.

selfTest.q: Does repeating the terminal return across tokens count the reward several times?
selfTest.a: No. It weights separate terms in the derivative of the sequence log probability. Do not also repeat the terminal reward in the reward-to-go calculation.

selfTest.q: What changes if terminal reward is discounted?
selfTest.a: Returns depend on the distance to termination. Derive the discounted objective and its score-function weights explicitly rather than broadcasting an undiscounted score.

selfTest.q: Why must changing finite padding log probabilities leave the loss unchanged?
selfTest.a: Padding is not a sampled action. The completion mask removes it from both the loss and its selected-log-probability gradient.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's terminal-reward REINFORCE loss, hand gradients and padding-invariance tests.
units.stopWhen: Your loss and selected-log-probability gradients match the fixed example, and you can explain why a variable-length token mean is a different weighting.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 4 reach derive and implement depth; the mini-project checks terminal credit and the exact reduction.

units.title: PPO-style RLHF with a value critic, and critic cost versus group sampling
outcomes: Derive prefix-value targets and token advantages for PPO-style RLHF with terminal rewards and KL shaping.
Explain the separate actor and critic losses and which rollout quantities stay fixed.
Compare critic state and fitting cost with extra group generation and verifier calls under a common budget.
units.why: A critic can exploit prefix information that a sequence baseline cannot. It also adds learned state and another failure mode; removing it trades that burden for sibling sampling, not free variance reduction.

next.note: Estimate a prompt baseline without fitting a value model.

study.title: RLHF Book: language PPO and value targets
study.locator: Chapter 6, Value Functions and PPO, Example: PPO, and Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Reuse the earlier GAE and PPO derivations. Concentrate on completion boundaries, KL-shaped returns and critic targets; use rollout-time values for actor advantages.

study.title: Lecture 4: PPO implementation and its cost
study.locator: Slides 16 to 28, 30 and 35: rollout tensors, targets, critic clipping, initialization and resident model state
study.depth: Slide 27's claim that a prediction close to the target is unaffected by value clipping is not general: the maximum can select the larger clipped error. Check both branches.

focus: The critic scores the prefix before the action, not the completed answer. Its target includes future outcome reward and future KL-shaped token rewards.
Freeze old values, returns and actor advantages during batch reuse. Keep unwhitened advantages for constructing critic targets; whitening actor weights must not alter those targets.

Build the state ledger using GPU memory: allocated, reserved, peak and memory models. A separate critic needs parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations; a shared value head changes the ledger and couples the losses.

Compare variance on the same task and sampling budget. A critic is not guaranteed to reduce it, and group baselines require extra generated tokens and scoring calls. TRL 1.15.0 has no `PPOTrainer`; this path is a scratch estimator.
units.reproduce: For a completed three-token response, use rewards `[0., 0., 2.]`, rollout-time prefix values `[0.5, 1., 1.5]`, zero terminal bootstrap and \(\gamma=\lambda=1\). Recover advantages `[1.5, 1., 0.5]` and value targets `[2., 2., 2.]`. Then hand-check optional critic clipping with old value 0, current value 1, target 1 and clip width 0.2: the maximum of the two half-squared errors is 0.32, not zero.
traps: Using the critic's newly fitted values to recompute advantages after every minibatch. The actor's fixed surrogate then changes underneath the optimizer.
Assuming every PPO implementation holds four independent full models. A verifier can replace the reward model, backbones can be shared and frozen models can be offloaded.
Adding a separate KL loss after already shaping the reward with the same penalty. That changes the objective and may double its influence.

selfTest.q: Why can advantages differ across tokens when there is only one terminal reward?
selfTest.a: Prefix values differ, and GAE combines different TD residuals. KL shaping can also introduce intermediate token rewards.

selfTest.q: Can an inaccurate fixed baseline bias terminal-return REINFORCE?
selfTest.a: Not if it depends only on the pre-action state and its gradient is excluded. Bootstrapped targets from an inaccurate critic can introduce bias; these are different mechanisms.

selfTest.q: Does the critic predict the verifier score alone?
selfTest.a: It predicts the specified future return. With KL shaping, that includes future KL penalties as well as the outcome score.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the value-based fixed-rollout estimator, critic-target oracle and critic-versus-group cost ledger.
units.stopWhen: Your three-token advantages and targets match the oracle, both critic-clipping branches are explained, and your cost ledger includes generation as well as model state.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 4 cover language PPO, critic targets and costs; the mini-project checks a value-based estimator without relying on a removed trainer.

units.title: Leave-one-out baselines and RLOO
outcomes: Derive the leave-one-out baseline's conditional independence and unbiased score-function estimator.
Implement prompt-grouped RLOO and distinguish it from centering by a mean that includes the current reward.
units.why: RLOO uses sibling completions as a prompt-specific baseline. Excluding the current reward is the part that preserves the expected REINFORCE gradient.

next.note: Separate group centering from standard-deviation scaling and clipping.

study.title: RLHF Book: RLOO algebra
study.locator: Chapter 6, REINFORCE Leave One Out (RLOO), equations 25 to 27 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Back to Basics: sequence REINFORCE and RLOO
study.locator: arXiv:2402.14740v2, Sections 2.2 and 2.3, printed pp. 5 to 6: sequence estimator, moving-average baseline and the unnumbered RLOO estimator
study.depth: Stop before Section 2.4. The paper's model-scale comparisons are evidence for its setup, not a guarantee that RLOO beats PPO on your task.

focus: For \(K>1\) independent completions of one prompt, \(b_i=(K-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}R_j\). Conditional on the prompt, sibling rewards do not depend on the current sampled completion.

The identity \(A_i=\frac{K}{K-1}(R_i-\bar R)\) makes the finite-sample correction explicit. Centering alone shrinks the expected raw-reward gradient by \((K-1)/K\) under the same independence assumptions.
Keep siblings grouped by prompt identity, not their position after shuffling. Treat KL-shaped rewards as fixed score-function weights; do not differentiate through the baseline.
units.reproduce: For one prompt with rewards `[0., 1., 2.]`, obtain leave-one-out baselines `[1.5, 1., 0.5]` and advantages `[-1.5, 0., 1.5]`. Enumerate all pairs of independent binary completions with success probability \(p=1/2\), reward equal to the sampled bit and score \(\partial_p\log\pi\). The expected two-sample RLOO estimate is 1; centering by the inclusive mean gives 0.5. Verify by exact enumeration on CPU, not a Monte Carlo run.
traps: Using the whole minibatch as the sibling group. Prompt difficulty then contaminates the intended per-prompt baseline.
Generating siblings by dependent selection and still invoking the independent-sample proof. Best-of-N winners and sampling without replacement need a different analysis.
Using a singleton group. Its leave-one-out denominator is zero; reject it or choose a separately specified baseline.

selfTest.q: Is detaching an inclusive batch mean enough to make it action-independent?
selfTest.a: No. Detachment removes an autodiff path, not statistical dependence on the current sampled reward.

selfTest.q: Why does the baseline term have zero expectation?
selfTest.a: Condition on the prompt and the independent siblings. Their baseline is fixed while the current completion's expected score is zero.

selfTest.q: Does RLOO need a learned value model?
selfTest.a: No. It uses extra completions and reward calls to estimate the baseline. Those calls still belong in the cost budget.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's RLOO baseline, prompt-regrouping tests and exact expected-gradient comparison.
units.stopWhen: Your leave-one-out and inclusive-mean estimates match the enumeration, and shuffling complete rollout records preserves prompt-specific advantages.

fit.note: The book's algebra and the original RLOO estimator cover the derivation; the mini-project provides independence and regrouping tests.

units.title: Grouped sampling, group-relative advantages, GRPO and degenerate groups
outcomes: Derive outcome-supervised group advantages and identify their differences from RLOO.
Implement a critic-free clipped loss that handles mixed and all-equal reward groups.
units.why: GRPO replaces a fitted critic with comparisons between sibling completions. Its useful signal depends on reward differences within a prompt, not just on average success.

next.note: Measure how the normalization changes prompt weighting.

study.title: RLHF Book: GRPO
study.locator: Chapter 6, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), equations 33 to 38 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: DeepSeekMath: original outcome-supervised GRPO
study.locator: arXiv:2402.03300v3, Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, equations 3 and 4, Figure 4 and the unnumbered outcome-advantage formula
study.depth: Stop before process supervision in Section 4.1.3. Keep the original token ratios and per-response means separate from later trainer defaults.

focus: For outcome rewards, broadcast \(A_i=(R_i-\bar R)/(s_R+\delta)\) to completion tokens. Specify population or sample standard deviation, a positive stabilizer and a minimum group size.
Group centering, standard-deviation scaling, ratio clipping, KL placement and aggregation are separate choices. The algorithm name alone does not specify your loss.

All-equal rewards give zero outcome advantages with a finite denominator. All-correct and all-wrong binary groups share that property, but require different data decisions. An explicit KL term can still supply gradients.
The original method removes the critic and GAE. It does not remove sibling generation, verification or the need to test loss gradients.
units.reproduce: On CPU, normalize rewards `[1., 1., 0., 0.]` with population standard deviation and stabilizer `1e-4`. Obtain advantages approximately `[0.99980004, 0.99980004, -0.99980004, -0.99980004]`. Repeat with sample standard deviation: magnitudes become approximately 0.86587543. All-zero and all-one groups must give finite zero advantages. Reject a singleton before computing a sample standard deviation.
traps: Treating normalized inclusive centering as the unbiased RLOO estimator. The random denominator adds another dependence on the sampled group.
Adding a stabilizer after division. It cannot repair a zero denominator or an already undefined singleton sample standard deviation.
Calling all-correct groups proof of generalization. The held-out prompt distribution may still fail.

selfTest.q: Does zero mean advantage imply zero policy gradient?
selfTest.a: No. Different completions have different score vectors. Their weighted gradients need not cancel.

selfTest.q: Does an all-wrong binary group identify the least wrong completion?
selfTest.a: No. Equal verifier rewards give no relative outcome information. Use a specified richer reward or change sampling, not an invented ranking.

selfTest.q: Why do NumPy and PyTorch ports sometimes disagree?
selfTest.a: Their default standard-deviation corrections differ. Specify the convention and stabilizer in both implementations.

practice.name: Normalize GRPO Group Advantages
practice.locator: Language Modeling from Scratch plan, Normalize GRPO Group Advantages: statement, function signature and public examples
practice.note: The problem uses population standard deviation. The section mini-project also tests sample-standard-deviation parity and degenerate groups.

units.stopWhen: Your mixed and all-equal groups match the specified convention, and you can list every choice needed to turn those advantages into a loss.

fit.note: The book and original paper cover the estimator and critic-free trade-off; the free TensorTonic problem and mini-project cover normalization and degenerate groups.

units.title: Within-prompt and batch normalization, reward scaling and comparability
outcomes: Derive how prompt-level and batch-level scaling reweight a fixed reward batch.
Measure advantage and gradient changes under reward shifts, rescaling and batch-composition changes.
units.why: Normalization is part of the estimator, not just numerical housekeeping. It can erase reward-scale differences or make one prompt's update depend on unrelated prompts.

next.note: Combine advantage weights with an explicit loss reduction.

study.title: Dr. GRPO: question-level weighting
study.locator: arXiv:2503.20783v2, Sections 3.1 and 3.2: Question-level difficulty bias, Figure 4 and removal of standard-deviation scaling
study.depth: Study the weighting argument, not the large-model experiment. Inclusive centering remains a scaled RLOO estimator; removing standard-deviation scaling alone does not make it exactly unbiased.

study.title: TRL 1.15.0: group and batch reward scaling
study.locator: Computing the advantage and `GRPOConfig`'s `scale_rewards` parameter
study.depth: Inspect only group, batch and disabled scaling. Batch scaling retains per-group centering; it is not global reward centering.

focus: Separate the scope of the mean from the scope of the standard deviation. Per-group centering with one batch scale differs from centering all rewards together.
With no stabilizer and nonzero variance, a positive affine reward transform leaves group z-scores unchanged. A stabilizer breaks exact scale invariance; a negative multiplier reverses signs.

For binary rewards with population success fraction \(p\), the group standard deviation is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}\). Rare successes and rare failures get large relative weights; exactly equal groups still have zero centered reward.

Measure selected-log-probability gradient norms as well as advantages. Whitening token advantages can weight long completions more in its statistics. Keep raw rewards and external quality for cross-run comparison.
units.reproduce: On CPU, use two prompt groups `[0., 2.]` and `[10., 14.]`. With population statistics and no stabilizer, group centering gives `[-1., 1.]` and `[-2., 2.]`; group scaling makes both `[-1., 1.]`. Per-group centering with batch standard deviation instead divides those centered values by `sqrt(32.75)`. Show that shifting only the second group leaves group z-scores unchanged but changes this batch scale. Use fixed token masks and score vectors to compare the resulting gradient weights.
traps: Comparing normalized training rewards across changing prompt mixtures as though they were absolute quality scores.
Claiming standard-deviation division always reduces variance. It changes relative weighting and can amplify noisy low-variance groups.
Whitening rewards, then whitening advantages again without recording both transformations.

selfTest.q: Does batch scaling erase the within-prompt baseline?
selfTest.a: Not in TRL's batch mode. It subtracts the group mean and uses a batch-level standard deviation.

selfTest.q: What does doubling raw reward do without standard-deviation scaling?
selfTest.a: It doubles centered outcome weights. If the KL coefficient stays fixed, the reward-to-KL balance changes too.

selfTest.q: Is a prompt's reward offset necessarily comparable with another prompt's offset?
selfTest.a: No. A preference-trained reward can have prompt-dependent offsets. Global centering may mix those offsets into the baseline.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's normalization ablation on fixed prompt groups, reward transforms and matched gradient reductions.
units.stopWhen: Your two-group oracle matches all three scaling choices, and the report separates raw reward, normalized advantage and external quality.

fit.note: Dr. GRPO supplies the weighting analysis and pinned TRL docs supply current normalization choices; the mini-project measures fixed-batch effects.

units.title: Token log probabilities, importance ratios, clipping and loss aggregation
outcomes: Implement detached old-policy token ratios and the sign-dependent clipped surrogate.
Derive the distinction between token surrogates and exact sequence importance weights.
Compare sequence means, token means and constant-denominator reductions on one frozen batch.
units.why: A correct ratio can still feed the wrong estimator. Token clipping and loss reduction control different parts of the update and must be tested separately.

next.note: Add the reference penalty and response-boundary contract.

study.title: RLHF Book: token ratios and loss reductions
study.locator: Chapter 6, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Understanding the PPO Objective, and Loss Aggregation Tradeoffs (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Reuse the earlier PPO clipping derivation. Clipping is a surrogate plateau, not a hard constraint on the updated policy. Compare reductions with identical token terms; the chapter's token-mean snippet omits the advantages used in its other two reductions.

study.title: DAPO: asymmetric clipping and token aggregation
study.locator: arXiv:2503.14476v2, Sections 3.1 and 3.3, equations 10 and 12
study.depth: Read the equations and weighting argument only. The paper's probability bounds describe clipping plateaus, not guaranteed bounds after an optimizer step.

focus: Compute \(\rho_{i,t}=\exp(\ell_{i,t}^{\text{current}}-\ell_{i,t}^{\text{old}})\) on identical sampled tokens and prefixes. Old log probabilities and advantages stay detached.

Maximize \(\min(\rho A,\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A)\). A positive advantage plateaus above the upper bound; a negative advantage plateaus below the lower bound. Other out-of-range cases still have gradients.

Exact trajectory reweighting uses \(\prod_t\rho_t\). A token ratio leaves the old prefix distribution in place; token PPO is a local surrogate, not exact off-policy correction of terminal sequence reward.

Name the denominator: response length then response mean, total valid tokens, or a fixed batch-size times generation limit. If group sizes vary, specify whether prompts or completions get equal weight. Accumulated token sums need a shared denominator to match a full-batch token mean.
units.reproduce: On CPU in `torch.float64`, use ratios `[0.5, 1.5, 0.5, 1.5]`, detached advantages `[2., 2., -2., -2.]` and clip width 0.2. The maximized terms are `[1., 2.4, -1.6, -3.]`; the negative mean loss is 0.3 and its gradients with respect to current selected log probabilities are `[-0.25, 0., 0., 0.75]`. Separately reduce token terms `[1., 1., 1., 1., 10.]` and `[1., 1., 1., 1., 1., 1., 1., 1., 1., 10.]`: sequence mean 2.35, token mean 2.2, constant denominator 20 gives 1.65.
traps: Clamping the ratio and discarding the minimum. This incorrectly removes corrective gradients on the wrong side of the interval.
Using reference log probabilities as old log probabilities. The reference anchor need not have generated the rollout.
Averaging token means from unequal minibatches. It does not recover the full-batch token mean unless token counts are equal or correctly weighted.

selfTest.q: Can every token ratio be inside the clip interval while the sequence ratio is outside?
selfTest.a: Yes. Two ratios of 1.1 multiply to 1.21, outside an interval with upper bound 1.2.

selfTest.q: Does a clipped token have no influence on any parameter update?
selfTest.a: Its active clipped outcome term has zero derivative away from a boundary. Other tokens, KL and shared parameters can still move its probability.

selfTest.q: Does TRL's dapo loss type select the complete DAPO recipe?
selfTest.a: No. It selects a reduction. Reward scaling, clipping bounds, KL and sampling need separate configuration.

practice.name: Compute a Clipped GRPO Surrogate
practice.locator: Language Modeling from Scratch plan, Compute a Clipped GRPO Surrogate: statement and public examples
practice.note: The problem reports out-of-range ratios, not the sign-dependent active plateau fraction. The section mini-project adds autodiff checks and unequal-length aggregation tests.

units.stopWhen: Both advantage signs match hand values and gradients, all three reductions match the frozen terms, and your minibatch reduction matches its stated full-batch objective.

fit.note: The book and DAPO cover clipping and reductions; the free TensorTonic surrogate problem and mini-project reach implementation depth.

units.title: Reference KL penalties, masks, truncated completions and length incentives
outcomes: Implement a reference-KL estimator with an explicit sampling distribution and reduction.
Test EOS, padding and length-limit boundaries without silently treating truncation as a completed answer.
Measure how masks, reward placement and normalization alter length incentives.
units.why: The reference penalty and response boundary are part of the objective. A plausible scalar KL or loss can hide a reversed ratio, a missing stopping action or an uncounted truncated output.

next.note: Check what stale sampling does to these estimators.

study.title: RLHF Book: reference KL
study.locator: Chapter 15, KL Divergence in RL Optimization, Reference Model to Generations and Implementation Example, equations 2 to 4 (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Stop before Other Tools to Control Optimization. The example passes two log tensors to `F.kl_div` without `log_target=True`; correct that and define the token reduction. Its sequence sum also needs a completion mask.

study.title: DAPO: truncated samples and length shaping
study.locator: arXiv:2503.14476v2, Section 3.4, Overlong Filtering and Soft Overlong Punishment, equation 13

study.title: TRL 1.15.0: KL and truncation configuration
study.locator: Estimating the KL divergence, Loss Types, and `GRPOConfig`'s `beta`, `mask_truncated_completions` and `use_bias_correction_kl` parameters
study.depth: Inspect these contracts only. A sampled KL value and its fixed-rollout gradient are different checks; record any correction for old-policy sampling.

focus: Build on Token entropy, sequence diversity, KL direction and KL estimators. Write \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\) instead of relying on forward or reverse labels. For current-policy samples with shared support, \(d=\log\pi_\theta-\log\pi_{\text{ref}}\) and \(\exp(-d)+d-1\) have the same KL expectation.

A detached rollout log-ratio can shape rewards; an explicit current-policy KL term has its own gradient. Neither estimator's value identity alone proves that fixed-old-sample autodiff equals the exact sequence-KL gradient.

Include sampled EOS when optimizing complete-sequence likelihood. Mask prompt tokens and post-EOS padding. A length-limit stop has no sampled EOS; retain its reason and choose a specified reward, bootstrap or loss-exclusion policy.

Per-token KL means and sequence KL sums have different length weighting. Dropping truncated losses changes the training population; log their rewards, lengths and cost even when their loss is masked. Measure length by correctness and validity, not just its overall mean.
units.reproduce: On CPU, enumerate a one-token policy `[0.75, 0.25]` and reference `[0.5, 0.5]`. Both the policy-weighted log ratio and the policy-weighted `exp(-d) + d - 1` give approximately 0.13081204 nats. Confirm with `torch.nn.functional.kl_div(reference.log(), policy.log(), reduction="sum", log_target=True)`. Then test completion records for immediate EOS, EOS followed by padding and length-limit truncation: only sampled actions enter the sequence likelihood, finite padding changes do not alter loss or gradients, and truncation remains a separate outcome.
traps: Using `exp(d) - d - 1` on policy samples as the same KL oracle. The probability ratio is reversed.
Interpreting a negative sampled log ratio as impossible KL. Individual log ratios can be negative; the exact expectation is nonnegative.
Discarding long failures, then reporting success only over the remaining outputs. That changes the evaluation denominator.

selfTest.q: Does a format-valid truncated answer necessarily have a terminal outcome reward?
selfTest.a: Only if the task contract scores that prefix as a valid answer. A generation cap alone does not establish completion or correctness.

selfTest.q: What if the policy places mass where the reference probability is zero?
selfTest.a: The policy-to-reference KL is infinite. Epsilon floors change that quantity and must not be hidden as exact KL.

selfTest.q: Does turning off the KL loss make reference-drift monitoring unnecessary?
selfTest.a: No. Loss regularization and diagnostic measurement are separate choices. TRL does not log its KL metric when `beta` is zero, so add an independent diagnostic if needed.

practice.name: Compare Sequence and Token Length Normalization
practice.locator: Language Modeling from Scratch plan, Compare Sequence and Token Length Normalization: statement and public examples
practice.note: The section mini-project extends this reduction check with reference-KL enumeration and EOS, padding and truncation cases.

units.stopWhen: Your enumerated KL matches the corrected library call, boundary tests pass, and every excluded completion remains visible in the cost and outcome ledger.

fit.note: The book, DAPO and pinned TRL docs cover KL and boundary choices; the free normalization problem and mini-project test reductions and masks.

units.title: Multiple gradient steps, off-policy drift, rollout freshness and policy lag
outcomes: Explain when batch reuse, minibatch updates and sampler lag make rollouts off-policy.
Measure ratio drift and effective sample size while preserving immutable behavior-policy log probabilities.
units.why: Freshness is a property of the policy and rollout record, not the wall clock alone. Rewriting old log probabilities can make a stale batch look perfectly on-policy.

next.note: Separate policy-lag defects from genuine loss of exploration.

study.title: RLHF Book: asynchronous rollouts and correction
study.locator: Chapter 6, Asynchronous RL Systems and Truncated Importance Sampling, Figures 8 and 9 and equations 48 to 50 (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the roles and log-probability ledger, not distributed deployment. A token correction does not fully correct the prefix distribution, and a cap introduces bias whose size is not guaranteed small.

study.title: Lecture 4: minibatch drift
study.locator: Slides 19 to 25: stored versus recomputed quantities and multiple epochs or minibatches
study.depth: Use the first-step argument, not slide 25's approximate six-epoch cutoff as a universal limit. Drift depends on update size, sampler and data.

focus: Freeze behavior weights and sampler settings during collection. Keep behavior log probabilities, old-checkpoint learner log probabilities and current learner log probabilities distinct when backends differ.

The first gradient evaluation has ratios 1 only when the actual behavior and current scoring policy match. Later minibatches can already be stale within the first epoch; gradient accumulation without intermediate steps does not create this parameter drift.

Log version lag, elapsed age, ratio quantiles, active clipping fraction and sequence-weight effective sample size. Reuse Support, coverage, effective sample size and visitation diagnostics; token ratios alone miss compounded sequence drift.

A fixed sampler-to-old-learner correction and the current-to-old-learner ratio address different mismatches. Truncating correction weights trades bias for stability. Bound queue age and refill attempts before considering a distributed system.
units.reproduce: On CPU, take a frozen one-token batch containing one example of each action from behavior policy `[0.5, 0.5]`. Score it under current policy `[0.8, 0.2]`: ratios are `[1.6, 0.4]`, empirical effective sample size is approximately 1.47058824 of 2, and exact current-to-behavior KL is approximately 0.19274476 nats. Overwriting old scores with current scores falsely returns `[1., 1.]` and effective sample size 2. Inject that overwrite and require a version-binding test to catch it.
traps: Treating one epoch as one optimizer step. Updates between minibatches can activate clipping within that epoch.
Refreshing old scores from newer weights to avoid large ratios. This erases the behavior distribution rather than correcting it.
Assuming matching version labels guarantees matching probabilities. Decoding transforms and backend numerics still need a parity check.

selfTest.q: Which policy belongs in an exact sequence importance denominator?
selfTest.a: The distribution that actually sampled that sequence, including its decoding transformation and support.

selfTest.q: Why record both elapsed age and version lag?
selfTest.a: Many updates can occur quickly, or none can occur during a long delay. The two measurements reveal different causes of staleness.

selfTest.q: Can importance weights recover actions excluded by top-p sampling?
selfTest.a: No. Missing behavior support cannot be recovered by reweighting the observed samples.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's immutable rollout versions, stale-score injection and CPU queue-age simulation.
units.stopWhen: The overwrite defect fails a test, the finite-policy drift metrics match, and the reuse policy names both its age limit and behavior-score provenance.

fit.note: The book and Lecture 4 explain sample reuse and backend mismatch; the mini-project measures drift without requiring distributed hardware.

units.title: Entropy collapse, KL spikes, invalid outputs, zero-signal groups and prompt balancing
outcomes: Measure entropy, KL, validity and zero-signal groups by prompt and outcome class.
Distinguish verifier failures, reward sparsity and policy contraction before changing sampling or curricula.
units.why: Zero-signal groups can mean mastery, failure or a broken verifier. A higher retained-batch reward cannot distinguish them, especially after prompt filtering.

next.note: Convert each diagnosed defect into a regression test.

study.title: DAPO: entropy, dynamic sampling and training diagnostics
study.locator: arXiv:2503.14476v2, Sections 3.1, 3.2 and 4.3, Figures 2, 3 and 7
study.depth: Study failure mechanisms and recorded metrics only. Dynamic sampling changes the retained prompt distribution; do not transfer the paper's wall-time conclusions to your small run.

study.title: TRL 1.15.0: diagnostic definitions
study.locator: Logged metrics: `entropy`, `reward`, `reward_std`, `frac_reward_zero_std`, `completions/clipped_ratio` and `clip_ratio` metrics
study.depth: Read metric definitions only. Zero reward standard deviation says nothing by itself about textual diversity or verifier correctness.

study.title: Post-Training Laboratory: failure evidence
study.locator: Architecture constraints, Milestone D - Failure handling, and Failure-injection requirements
study.depth: Use only the online-policy and verifier failures here. The full laboratory is a later integration, not this card's assignment.

focus: Reuse verifier soundness and outcome-class tests. Separate correct, incorrect, malformed, truncated and verifier-error records. A verifier timeout is missing evidence, not automatically a wrong answer.

Read token entropy alongside duplicate completions, distinct answers, reference KL, behavior-policy drift, length and held-out quality. Changing visited prefixes can change the mean entropy; use a fixed diagnostic prefix set as well.

For independent binary outcomes with success probability \(p\) and group size \(G\), mixed-group probability is \(1-p^G-(1-p)^G\). Rejecting equal groups favors intermediate success probabilities and consumes attempts even when no update follows.

Log original and retained prompt mixtures, all-correct and all-wrong fractions, acceptance rate and generation or verifier cost. Set a refill cap and a no-update fallback. Tune difficulty or sampling on validation evidence, not final evaluation.
units.reproduce: On CPU, enumerate four independent binary rewards. Mixed-group probability is 0.875 at success probability 0.5 and 0.3438 at success probability 0.1. Check the formula against the enumeration. Then replay records with equal rewards but distinct texts, identical texts, malformed outputs and verifier errors. Require separate diagnostic flags: equal reward is not itself entropy collapse, and verifier failure is not evidence of task failure.
traps: Calling all-correct and all-wrong groups the same failure because both have zero advantage. Their evaluation outcomes are opposite.
Increasing temperature to fix a verifier outage. Sampling cannot repair missing or incorrect labels.
Using an unbounded refill loop when every prompt has equal rewards. It can spend the whole budget without taking a step.

selfTest.q: Does zero reward variance imply identical completions?
selfTest.a: No. Different completions can receive the same binary or saturated reward. Measure output diversity separately.

selfTest.q: Why can higher entropy be bad?
selfTest.a: It may reflect incoherent or repetitive generation rather than useful exploration. Check independent quality and validity.

selfTest.q: What should a KL spike trigger before a hyperparameter change?
selfTest.a: Check policy and reference identity, masks, log-probability direction, numerical health and sampler parity. Then inspect fresh outputs and update size.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's zero-signal and verifier-failure replay, prompt-slice diagnostics and bounded refill accounting.
units.stopWhen: Your diagnostics separate each replayed failure class, mixed-group enumeration matches, and the refill cap preserves all attempted prompts and their costs.

fit.note: DAPO supplies sampling and collapse mechanisms, TRL defines metrics, and the laboratory plus mini-project supply verifier and retention failures.

units.title: Fixed-rollout estimator, ratio, clipping and gradient tests
outcomes: Build independent scalar-value and gradient oracles for value-based and critic-free losses.
Differential-test a pinned implementation only after matching its masks, normalization and KL convention.
units.why: A training curve is a weak loss test. Frozen rollouts let you isolate sign, detachment, mask and version errors before generation adds noise.

next.note: Use the tested estimator in a controlled behavior study.

study.title: RLHF Book: fixed loss implementations
study.locator: Chapter 6, Example: PPO and Example: GRPO, then Suggested Experiments (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the loss equations as references for your own fixtures. Match each reduction explicitly and keep rollout-time advantages fixed.

study.title: Pinned policy-gradient losses: differential reference
study.locator: Commit 1042143, `masked_mean`, `ReinforceLoss`, `PPOLoss`, `GRPOLoss`, `DAPOLoss` and `approx_kl1`/`approx_kl3`
study.depth: Compare outcome losses with KL disabled first. `ReinforceLoss` uses a per-response token mean, not the sequence sum taught earlier. For policy-sampled policy-to-reference KL, `approx_kl1` has the opposite sign and `approx_kl3` the reversed ratio; do not adopt them as independent KL oracles.

focus: Reuse the earlier hand fixtures. Test selected-log-probability gradients before model-parameter gradients, then check a tiny differentiable categorical policy against exact enumeration.

At an identical behavior checkpoint, the differentiable ratio is numerically 1 but has derivative 1 with respect to current log probability. Replacing it with a literal constant kills the gradient. With matching weights and reduction, its first-step outcome gradient equals REINFORCE's, not necessarily its scalar loss.

Check padding invariance, prompt exclusion, EOS inclusion, reward detachment, group permutation, fixed old scores, clipping for both signs and finite all-equal groups. Reject invalid empty masks and singleton groups according to the loss contract.

Use float64 CPU arithmetic and finite differences away from clipping kinks. Then add a framework differential test with explicit TRL 1.15.0 settings; its default token-mean reduction and zero KL coefficient do not reproduce original GRPO.
units.reproduce: On CPU, let current selected log probability be a scalar leaf initialized to -1, old log probability be its detached clone, and detached advantage be 2. The negative clipped surrogate at ratio 1 has value -2 and derivative -2 with respect to the current log probability. The negative log-probability REINFORCE loss has value 2 and the same derivative -2. Show that a literal ratio of 1 has no current-log-probability gradient, while `exp(logp - logp.detach())` does. Extend this test with the earlier clipping, RLOO, normalization and KL fixtures.
traps: Checking only scalar equality. Detached current scores can reproduce the same loss while giving no policy gradient.
Differential-testing two implementations that share the same helper bug. Keep hand arithmetic or exact enumeration independent.
Using an empty-mask denominator guard to silently accept invalid data. A finite zero loss is not evidence of a valid rollout.

selfTest.q: Why can a zero centered loss still have nonzero gradients?
selfTest.a: Centered advantages can sum to zero while weighting different score vectors. Scalar cancellation does not imply gradient cancellation.

selfTest.q: Should old scores receive gradients during batch reuse?
selfTest.a: No. They define the fixed behavior denominator. Only the current policy scores are differentiated in that ratio.

selfTest.q: What must be matched before a library loss is a useful differential reference?
selfTest.a: Selected tokens, masks, old scores, advantages, clipping bounds, KL estimator and sampling assumptions, and all reduction denominators.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's value-based and critic-free estimator suites, first-step gradient equivalence and deliberate ratio, mask and version defects.
units.stopWhen: Hand and autodiff values and gradients agree, every injected defect fails a named test, and library differences are explained by explicit contracts rather than hidden defaults.

fit.note: The book and pinned code provide inspectable loss references; the mini-project supplies independent oracles and regression tests rather than trusting source helpers.

units.title: SFT, DPO, rejection and best-of-N controls, matched budgets and training traces
outcomes: Compare a small online policy update with SFT, DPO, rejection fine-tuning and inference-time selection controls.
Account for generated tokens, verifier calls, updates and wall time, including failed and filtered attempts.
Interpret reward and independent quality traces with KL, entropy, length, validity and prompt-level uncertainty.
units.why: Online RL can spend much more sampling compute than its controls. The evidence must distinguish learned behavior from extra candidates, a permissive verifier or a changed evaluation denominator.

next.note: Carry the objective tests and evidence ledger into a prespecified extension.

study.title: DeepSeekMath: controls and sampling versus improvement
study.locator: arXiv:2402.03300v3, Sections 5.2.1 and 5.2.2, Table 10 and Figures 5 and 7
study.depth: Read the control definitions and evaluation distinction only. These comparisons do not establish an algorithm ranking under your budgets; DPO is a preference objective, not an on-policy policy-gradient estimator.

study.title: Post-Training Laboratory: matched evidence
study.locator: Hardware variants, Milestones B, E and F, Measurement requirements and Design-defense questions
study.depth: Apply these standards to the section's reduced-scale online study, not the entire laboratory. Reuse earlier SFT, DPO, verifier and evaluation components.

study.title: TRL 1.15.0: trace definitions
study.locator: Logged metrics: `num_tokens`, `step_time`, `reward`, `entropy`, `kl`, completion length and clipping metrics
study.depth: Use definitions, not the eight-GPU Quick start. `num_tokens` includes prompts and completions; add separate generated-token and verifier-call counters.

focus: Use a tiny CPU text policy and short verifiable completions first. If your GPU fits weights, optimizer state, activations and generation buffers, repeat with a small decoder or adapter. Frozen rollouts establish loss correctness, not online behavior improvement.

Start controls from the same checkpoint and prompt split. SFT imitates specified targets; DPO uses scored pairs; rejection fine-tuning imitates accepted samples; best-of-N selects without updating weights. Name the selector available at deployment and any oracle-only upper bound.

Reuse Matched interaction and compute budgets, tuning budgets and final-evaluation isolation. Match a prespecified main budget axis and disclose the others; equal updates do not imply equal tokens or compute. Count collection, retries, rejected groups, verification, training and evaluation separately.

Plot raw reward, independent quality, reference KL, token entropy, length, validity and signal coverage against both consumed budget and update count. Evaluate fresh held-out outputs at common decoding settings and selection budgets. Pair by prompt and report seed spread or prompt-level uncertainty; preserve failures and reward-hacking probes.
units.reproduce: Audit a CPU fixture with three prompts, four generated completions per prompt and completion lengths `[5, 6, 7, 8]` for each prompt. Score every completion once and retain six for training. The collection ledger must still show 78 generated tokens, 12 verifier calls and 12 attempted completions, with six retained. Use that accounting rule in the mini-project's bounded online study. Compare fresh held-out outputs before and after training with the named controls; report a gain, no detectable gain or a regression without requiring a particular score.
traps: Calling a best-of-N gain a learned policy improvement. Selection changes the delivered answer without changing model weights.
Building DPO pairs with extra uncounted generations or charging only the accepted samples in rejection fine-tuning.
Choosing checkpoints or reward parameters on the final held-out score. The final evaluation then becomes tuning data.

selfTest.q: What would support learned improvement rather than extra inference compute?
selfTest.a: Fresh outputs from the updated policy outperform the starting policy at the same decoding and selection budget on independent held-out evaluation. Matched training controls strengthen attribution.

selfTest.q: Is rising training reward with flat external quality a successful result?
selfTest.a: It shows proxy fitting, not established behavior improvement. Inspect hacking, validity, length and evaluation uncertainty.

selfTest.q: Must every control consume identical wall time and token counts?
selfTest.a: Usually that is infeasible. Choose the main matching axis in advance, disclose all costs and compare quality-cost trade-offs rather than claiming universal superiority.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's tiny online update, matched SFT and direct-preference controls, rejection and best-of-N comparison, complete traces and reward-hacking evidence pack.
units.stopWhen: The cost fixture balances, controls disclose every budget axis, and fresh independent evaluation supports a hardware-scoped conclusion with failed attempts and uncertainty retained.

fit.note: DeepSeekMath defines the controls, the laboratory sets the evidence standard and TRL defines traces; the mini-project integrates them at reduced scale.
